questions.q: What does the redirect_uri parameter specify in an OAuth flow?
o: Where the provider should send the user and the authorization code
The list of scopes the client wants the resource owner to approve
The API path used later to fetch the user profile document
The secret used by the provider to sign issued access tokens
questions.x: After the user authenticates, the OAuth provider redirects the browser to redirect_uri and attaches the authorization code. That URL is where the code is delivered.
questions.h: After consent, the browser is sent somewhere with a code. Which parameter names that destination?

questions.q: How does secure redirect_uri handling differ from a vulnerable one?
o: Secure handling requires HTTPS, while vulnerable handling allows HTTP
Secure handling allows only pre-registered URLs, not attacker-chosen ones
Secure handling encrypts the code, vulnerable handling does not
Secure handling uses POST redirects, while vulnerable handling uses GET
questions.x: A secure provider only redirects to URLs registered for that client, such as the real app callback. A vulnerable provider redirects to whatever URL the attacker supplies, so the code lands on the attacker site.
questions.h: The fix is validation. What set of URLs should be the only ones a provider will redirect to?

questions.q: Why is a stolen authorization code so dangerous?
o: The code is a long-lived password for the authorization server itself
The code never expires, so it can be replayed against any OAuth client
Authorization codes are bearer tokens, so whoever has the code can use it
The code includes the user password in a claim the client must echo
questions.x: Authorization codes are bearer tokens. Possession is enough. Whoever intercepts the code can exchange it for access to the victim account, much like finding another person's car keys.
questions.h: Bearer means possession is enough. If the code arrives at the attacker server, what can they do with it?

questions.q: What happens if an attacker can set redirect_uri to a site they control?
o: The provider refuses to issue a code until the real app also consents
The victim code is delivered to the attacker instead of the real app
The access token is encrypted so the attacker site cannot read it
The client_secret is rotated automatically before the code is issued
questions.x: The provider sends the browser, and the authorization code, to the attacker URL. The attacker then holds the code and can try to exchange it for access to the victim account.
questions.h: The code follows redirect_uri. If that URI is the attacker site, who receives the code?

questions.q: What should an OAuth provider do with redirect_uri before redirecting?
o: Sign it with HS256 so the client can verify the callback host
Open it in a new window so the original app cannot see the code
Append the user password so the client can finish local login
Accept it only if it matches a URL already registered for that client
questions.x: The provider should compare redirect_uri to pre-registered URLs for that client. If any attacker-supplied URL is accepted, the authorization code is delivered to the wrong place.
questions.h: Secure handling is a comparison against a known list. What is on that list?
